meta.title: Relay
meta.subtitle: How a parcel gets from a merchant's shelf to a doorstep, and what holds that together

sections.title: The shape of it
sections.summary: What runs, and why there are three front doors instead of one.
sections.narrative:
Relay has three kinds of user and almost nothing in common between them. A merchant integrates once and calls an API for years. A recipient arrives from an SMS, has no account, and will never come back. A courier is offline half the day and uploads in bursts.

That is why there are three front doors rather than one, and why each authenticates differently: an API key for merchants [[auth.merchant-key]], a one-time code for recipients [[auth.recipient-otp]], a client certificate for handhelds [[auth.handheld-mtls]]. Trying to serve all three from one authenticated API is the mistake this architecture exists to avoid.

Behind them, one service owns parcel state [[dispatch.owns-state]] and one service owns the write path for movement [[scans.only-writer]]. Everything else reads.

sections.title: What actually moves a parcel
sections.summary: The one rule that makes the status field mean something.
sections.narrative:
**Only a scan moves a parcel forward.** There is no manual status edit anywhere in Relay [[state.no-manual-edit]], and the transition table is enforced in code rather than by convention [[state.table-enforced]].

This is not fussiness. A status that a human could set by hand would not be evidence that a parcel was physically anywhere, and every downstream promise — the delivery window, the merchant's invoice, the insurance claim — is built on it being exactly that.

The cost is that a parcel with a broken barcode is genuinely stuck until someone scans it, and support cannot type their way out. That trade is deliberate.

> Two attempts, then the parcel stops moving until a person chooses [[policy.two-attempts]]. Van time is the scarce resource here, not shelf space at a depot, so a third speculative attempt costs more than waiting.

sections.title: Scans arrive late and out of order
sections.summary: The assumption that shapes ingest, and the bug it prevents.
sections.narrative:
A handheld in a depot basement holds its scans and uploads when it finds signal. So a batch can contain scans older than ones already recorded, and the same batch can arrive twice when an upload times out on a bad connection.

Both are handled at the ingest boundary. Every scan carries a key that is stable across retries, and a unique index is what enforces exactly-once — a duplicate loses the race and is discarded [[scans.idempotent]]. A scan describing a step the parcel has already passed is still recorded, because the history has to be complete, but it does not move the status backwards [[state.no-backwards]].

The practical consequence for anyone reading this data: `scanned_at` is device time and can be wrong [[scans.device-clock]], while `received_at` is set by the server and cannot be [[scans.server-clock]]. Order a tracking history by the first and reason about lateness with the second.

sections.title: The API surface
sections.summary: Every operation, grouped by who is allowed to call it.
sections.narrative: Cancellation is the one merchant operation with a hard edge: it is only honoured before the first scan [[cancel.before-first-scan]]. After that the parcel exists in the network and has to come back through it, which is a return and is charged as one.

glossary.definition: A barcode read by a courier's handheld. The only evidence Relay accepts that a parcel was physically somewhere.
A sorting site. Every parcel passes through at least one, usually two.
A vehicle moving parcels between depots rather than to doorsteps.
One parcel's place in a driver's sequenced day, with the two-hour window promised to the recipient.

out_of_scope.reason: How a shipment becomes a line on a merchant's bill is owned by the finance platform and documented there. Nothing here describes rate cards or surcharges.
The routing engine's algorithm is not documented here. This document says a route gets sequenced; it does not say how.
Not documented yet. Parcels for postcodes Relay does not serve leave the network and the tracking history goes quiet, and no claim here explains what happens to them.
A lost parcel opens a claim. The claims process itself lives with the commercial team and is not modelled in this system.
Client certificates are issued and rotated by field systems. Nothing here covers enrolment, revocation, or what happens to a stolen device.
